explicit_evidence_changes.baseline: Deepfake videos falsely depicted clinicians from Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust endorsing weight-loss patches and misleading medical claims. The identifiable clinicians had not endorsed the products, and the trust publicly warned that the advertisements were false; the reviewed sources did not identify purchaser financial loss or medical injury.
explicit_evidence_changes.candidate: Videos circulating on social media promoted weight-loss patches through supposed doctors claiming affiliation with Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust. The Trust said the people named and pictured were not its staff and the endorsements were fraudulent. It warned the public on 9 January2026 and said it was seeking removal. Full Fact later reported fake names and images, misleading hospital branding and thousands of Facebook views. Its checks identified signs of AI generation; purchaser losses and medical injuries were not reported.

baseline.factual_basis: BBC reporting and the trust warning describe manipulated videos that used identifiable clinicians' likenesses and voices to promote weight-loss patches. The clinicians had not endorsed the products. The trust warned the public that the advertisements were false; the reviewed evidence does not establish a purchaser's financial loss or medical injury.
baseline.governance_interpretation: The advertisements appropriated clinician identity and authority for false endorsements. That identity and agency failure is supported. Exact AI-awareness disclosures remain unresolved. The trust’s warning does not establish takedown, purchaser loss or medical injury.
baseline.significance_to_cam: The case shows that synthetic medical impersonation can transfer trusted clinical authority into advertising, creating dignitary injury and a risk of consequential health reliance even where downstream injury is not yet evidenced.
assessment_boundaries: The first circulation date is not public; the record uses the earliest supported warning/reporting date.
No reviewed source establishes a realised health injury or purchase loss.

candidate.factual_basis: The originating Trust warning and Full Fact response identify fictional doctor names/images and false institutional affiliation. They do not identify an appropriated real clinician’s likeness or voice. Full Fact describes fabricated hospital signage, including separate Mayo Clinic branding, circulation and attributed watermark checks. A reported positive watermark check on one video does not attribute every video to a generator; non-detection on another does not exclude AI. The warning and request for takedown do not establish completed removal, purchases or injury. Health efficacy was outside Full Fact’s adjudication.
candidate.governance_interpretation: False medical and institutional authority supplied commercial solicitation and deceptive trust cues. A generator-side authority failure over a real identifiable person is not established and its former mapping is withdrawn. Institutional false attribution and public correction remain material. Human promotional intent is not an independently pursued model objective. Warning and removal efforts are distinct from successful containment.
candidate.significance_to_cam: Fictional professional identities can borrow real institutional trust to influence health-related purchases. Institutional impersonation, real-person likeness appropriation and verified purchaser harm require separate evidence.
